# AHSEF Stage 3 — results: dynamic Text → Audio acquisition

*Experiment `stage3_text_audio_v1`. Every number in this document is read from a JSON artefact under `experiments/ahsef/stage3_text_audio/`; the document is generated by `python -m src.ahsef.cli.run_stage3_text_audio --stage report` and is not written by hand.*

Method and design decisions: `docs/ahsef_stage3_text_audio.md`.

## 1. The aligned Text+Audio pool (Phase A)

Stage 1 established that the only defensible co-split pair in this project is
Text + Audio. Phase A turns that pair into an exact sample list and records the
evidence that vetted it.

| Split | Samples | Fingerprint | Datasets | Labels agreed | Train contamination |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| validation | 509 | c4715026f4d164b6 | MSP-Podcast=509 | 509 | none |
| test | 482 | c44ed7e03972e774 | MSP-Podcast=482 | 482 | none |

Verified:

- identical sample ids in both modality manifests
- identical split assignment (co-split rule)
- no train/validation/test contamination
- compatible seven-class emotion label space
- agreeing ground truth for every pooled id
- provenance recorded for both modalities
- record-level availability of both modality payloads

Explicitly not done:

- the pool was NOT expanded by joining ids across different splits
- no synthetic alignment was created
- no cross-corpus pairing (audio+video, audio+image, audio+physiology) was fabricated

**Limitation.** Both splits are drawn entirely from MSP-Podcast, the only corpus in this project carrying audio and text on the same record within one split. Stage 3 results therefore describe a Text->Audio routing policy on conversational podcast speech, not a corpus-general one.

Validation class balance:

| Class | neutral | happy | sad | angry | fear | disgust | surprise |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| n | 172 | 151 | 63 | 95 | 6 | 7 | 15 |

The three rarest classes carry single-digit support. Every macro-averaged
figure in this document is therefore dominated at the margin by a handful of
samples, and per-class F1 for `fear`, `disgust`, and `surprise` should be read
as an indication rather than a measurement.

## 3. HSIG: can the gain be predicted? (Phase D)

Target: `gain(m | A) = P(correct | A u {m}) - P(correct | A)`, estimated on validation only.
Positive events (`y_gain`): 34 of 509 (6.7%). Harmful events (`y_harm`): 13 (2.6%).

**Every figure below is out of fold.** At this pool size an in-sample AUROC
would be optimistic by an amount that changes the conclusion, so the model is
scored by 5-fold seeded stratified cross-validation,
and every reference -- a constant at the base rate, a shallow forest, and the
single-feature variants -- is scored by the same code path.

| Estimator | AUROC | AUROC 95% CI | AUPRC | AUPRC baseline | Spearman ρ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `paired_logistic__uncertainty_only` | 0.7555 | [0.659, 0.839] | 0.2159 | 0.067 | 0.126 |
| `fix_logistic__uncertainty_only` | 0.7564 | [0.662, 0.839] | 0.2148 | 0.067 | 0.130 |
| `paired_logistic__evidence_only` | 0.7199 | [0.625, 0.808] | 0.1689 | 0.067 | 0.093 |
| `fix_logistic__evidence_only` | 0.7235 | [0.622, 0.814] | 0.1708 | 0.067 | 0.109 |
| `paired_logistic__evidence_plus_class` | 0.6694 | [0.543, 0.790] | 0.1651 | 0.067 | 0.134 |
| `fix_logistic__evidence_plus_class` | 0.6912 | [0.574, 0.805] | 0.1855 | 0.067 | 0.103 |
| `prior_constant` | 0.5000 | [0.500, 0.500] | 0.0526 | 0.067 | -- |
| `shallow_forest_reference` | 0.6425 | [0.512, 0.768] | 0.1709 | 0.067 | 0.037 |

**Verdict.** fix_logistic__evidence_only reaches AUROC 0.7235 against fix_logistic__uncertainty_only's 0.7564; the 95% bootstrap interval of the candidate CONTAINS the reference value, so this pool cannot establish that the learned estimator beats the simple reference. The routing result must be read with that in mind.

Frozen estimator: `paired_logistic` over feature set `uncertainty_only`, fingerprint `96988c45c9dbcd28`.

### How that variant was chosen

- **Primary rule.** highest out-of-fold AUROC against y_gain on validation. Best by that rule: `fix_logistic__uncertainty_only` at AUROC 0.7564.
- **Tie-break.** among variants whose AUROC falls inside the bootstrap 95% interval of the best -- that is, variants this pool cannot distinguish -- prefer 'paired_logistic'.
- Variants this pool cannot distinguish from the best: `fix_logistic__evidence_only`, `fix_logistic__evidence_plus_class`, `fix_logistic__uncertainty_only`, `paired_logistic__evidence_only`, `paired_logistic__evidence_plus_class`, `paired_logistic__uncertainty_only`
- Selected `paired_logistic__uncertainty_only` at AUROC 0.7555, conceding 0.0009 AUROC to the tie-break.

UGAPR computes J = gain - lambda*C - mu*L, so the gain has to be in the units the target is defined in: a DIFFERENCE of probabilities of being correct. paired_logistic emits exactly that. fix_logistic emits P(audio fixes a wrong answer), which lives in [0, 1], is a different quantity, and cannot express harm at all -- subtracting a cost from it would be a category error dressed as a utility. The preference is therefore a property of the estimator's output, not of its score on this pool.

Features driving the acquisition decision (standardised weights on the
difference of the two components -- positive means acquiring looks more
attractive as the feature rises):

| Feature | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| `uncertainty` | 0.165 |

**Is this a hard-coded class rule in disguise?**
Within-class spread of predicted gain: 0.0219; between-class spread: 0.0259.
The estimator's feature set contains no class indicator, so it cannot be a class lookup as a matter of construction: it never sees the predicted class. Any between-class variation below is an image of how uncertainty itself differs across the classes the LLM predicts, not a rule keyed on the class.

**Caveat.** The estimator is fitted on 509 validation samples with 1 feature and 34 positive events. Bootstrap intervals are reported for every headline statistic because a point estimate at this size would invite a conclusion the data cannot carry.

## 4. The frozen configuration (Phases E, F, J)

Frozen at `2026-08-30T10:35:06`, git commit `519b9c2e31b2`.

### Gate objective

    utility = macro_f1 - alpha * acquisition_rate - beta * normalized_latency

Selected objective: `macro_f1_acquisition_latency`, α = 0.05, β = 0.02, τ = 0.094797.

Stage 2 showed that an accuracy-shaped objective on this corpus selects a neutral-heavy operating point with substantially higher accuracy and catastrophically lower macro-F1. Macro-F1 weights every emotion equally, so a policy cannot buy utility by ignoring the minority classes. The acquisition and latency penalties are what make the objective a ROUTING objective rather than a pure accuracy objective: without them the optimum is trivially 'always acquire'.

The alternatives were swept and are recorded so the choice is auditable:

| Objective | τ | Acquisition rate | Accuracy | Macro-F1 | Selected |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `accuracy` | -0.0412 | 100.0% | 0.5128 | 0.3510 | no |
| `macro_f1` | 0.0948 | 10.6% | 0.4872 | 0.3536 | no |
| `balanced_accuracy` | 0.0948 | 10.6% | 0.4872 | 0.3536 | no |
| `macro_f1_acquisition` | 0.0948 | 10.2% | 0.4872 | 0.3536 | no |
| `macro_f1_acquisition_latency` | 0.0948 | 10.2% | 0.4872 | 0.3536 | **yes** |

### UGAPR

    J(m) = gain_hat(m) - lambda * C(m) - mu * L(m)

λ = 0.1, μ = 0.1, candidate registry = ['audio'], audio penalty = 0.000812.

| Modality | Latency (ms) | Compute units | Normalised cost | Normalised latency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| audio | 27.9 | 9.07e+08 | 0.0000 | 0.0081 |
| image | 17.8 | 1.22e+10 | 0.0005 | 0.0052 |
| physiology | 0.1 | 4.45e+05 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |
| text | 19.8 | 2.71e+08 | 0.0000 | 0.0057 |
| text_llm | 3449.7 | 2.24e+13 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| video | 411.0 | 9.8e+10 | 0.0044 | 0.1191 |

Ollama cloud throughput is not constant: Stage 2 recorded an 18x swing within one run. The recorded latency is the mean measured during the Stage 3 pass and is a point estimate of a varying quantity, not a service guarantee.

### Threshold selection: which scores τ was chosen against

tau thresholds a specific function's output. Out-of-fold scores come from K separately fitted models and are a different random variable, so a tau calibrated on them selects a different -- and on this pool a measurably worse -- set of samples when applied to the deployed estimator. HSIG QUALITY is still reported out of fold; only the operating point is chosen against the function it will be applied to.

| Scores τ was chosen on | τ | Acquisition rate | Macro-F1 | Accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Deployed estimator (frozen)** | 0.094797 | 10.2% | 0.3536 | 0.4872 |
| Out-of-fold (comparison only) | 0.090078 | 12.6% | 0.3599 | 0.4912 |

What the same objective would have chosen from out-of-fold scores. Recorded so the optimism of selecting one scalar in-sample can be read off rather than taken on trust.

Everything the locked test evaluation depends on is fixed here. --stage test loads this file, verifies every value against the requested configuration and against the HSIG fingerprint on disk, and never writes it. Refitting HSIG, reselecting tau, retuning a fusion weight, or changing lambda/mu/alpha/beta after this point invalidates the evaluation and the test stage refuses to proceed.

A dynamic policy earns its complexity only if it sits ABOVE the line joining text-only to always-fusion on these axes. Sitting on or below that line means the same performance was available by acquiring at random, or by not routing at all.

A dynamic policy earns its complexity only if it sits ABOVE the line joining text-only to always-fusion on these axes. Sitting on or below that line means the same performance was available by acquiring at random, or by not routing at all.


**Reading.** G above D is the evidence that a learned gain estimate beats an uncertainty trigger. G below F says how much of the achievable gain a real estimator captures. G against C says what routing costs in performance and saves in acquisition. If G does not sit above D, the honest conclusion is that HSIG adds nothing over Stage 2's signal on this pool.

**D (uncertainty threshold), E (HSIG without UGAPR) and G (HSIG + UGAPR) select the identical sample set. Two facts explain it, and both are measurements from this run rather than assumptions. First, the frozen HSIG variant is the one fitted on the single feature 'uncertainty', because the richer feature sets did not predict the gain better out of fold -- so thresholding its output is thresholding a transform of uncertainty. Second, the UGAPR penalty is 8.12e-04, four orders of magnitude below the gain scale, because audio is genuinely cheap beside a 32.7B cloud LLM; it cannot move a decision. The honest reading is that on this pool AHSEF's advantage over Stage 2 comes from the REDESIGNED OBJECTIVE, not from a richer evidence model or from the cost term.**

### What the locked test does and does not establish

**Did the router acquire on better-than-random samples?**

Yes. 9 of 46 paid acquisitions fixed a wrong text answer (19.6%) against a population base rate of 7.1%, a lift of 2.8x. HSIG's out-of-sample AUROC on the locked split is 0.7408, so the estimator fitted on validation does transfer.

**Did that targeting beat acquiring at random at the same rate?**

NO, not on macro-F1. AHSEF's macro-F1 of 0.3350 falls INSIDE the 95% interval of random acquisition at the same rate [0.3117, 0.3556] and is below the random mean of 0.3368. The locked test does not establish a system-level macro-F1 advantage for intelligent routing over random routing at the same budget.

**How does it sit against text-only and full fusion?**

AHSEF retains 97.9% of always-fusion's macro-F1 and 93.3% of its accuracy while acquiring audio for 9.5% of samples instead of 100%. Against text-only it gains +0.0124 accuracy and +0.0005 macro-F1. Always-fusion remains the best system on both metrics: if audio can be afforded for every sample, acquiring it for every sample is the better policy on this pool.

**Validation → test.** On validation the same policy reached macro-F1 0.3536 against a random control mean of 0.3134, clearly outside the control interval. That advantage did not replicate on the locked test. The threshold was selected on validation labels, so the validation figure carries selection optimism that the locked figure does not; the gap between them is the size of that optimism and is reported rather than explained away.

## 8. The scientific claim (Phase L)

The defensible claim is:

> AHSEF dynamically determines whether additional audio evidence is worth acquiring after an initial LLM-based text assessment, using a validation-trained expected-gain estimator and a cost/latency-aware utility policy.

This is a Text->Audio proof of concept. It is NOT a demonstration that AHSEF selects the best modality among all modalities: the available corpora provide no sample with two simultaneously available candidates, so the candidate set has exactly one member. Physiology is a separate 3-class task and is never fused into the 7-class emotion task.

Specifically **not** claimed:

- that AHSEF selects the best modality among all modalities. The candidate
  set has one member, so no selection among modalities was tested.
- that the result generalises beyond conversational podcast speech. Both
  splits are drawn entirely from MSP-Podcast, the only corpus in this project
  carrying audio and text on the same record within one split.
- that the LLM's class scores are posteriors. Stage 2 measured their NLL as
  worse than uniform; they are normalised self-reports throughout.

On whether the learned estimator beats a simple baseline:

> fix_logistic__evidence_only reaches AUROC 0.7235 against fix_logistic__uncertainty_only's 0.7564; the 95% bootstrap interval of the candidate CONTAINS the reference value, so this pool cannot establish that the learned estimator beats the simple reference. The routing result must be read with that in mind.

On what the locked test established:

> Yes. 9 of 46 paid acquisitions fixed a wrong text answer (19.6%) against a population base rate of 7.1%, a lift of 2.8x. HSIG's out-of-sample AUROC on the locked split is 0.7408, so the estimator fitted on validation does transfer.

> NO, not on macro-F1. AHSEF's macro-F1 of 0.3350 falls INSIDE the 95% interval of random acquisition at the same rate [0.3117, 0.3556] and is below the random mean of 0.3368. The locked test does not establish a system-level macro-F1 advantage for intelligent routing over random routing at the same budget.

Read together, the two findings say that the *targeting* component works and the *end-to-end benefit over a random budget* is not established on this pool. Both belong in the claim, and neither cancels the other.
